topics.title: Drug Metabolism: Phase I & Phase II
topics.productionRationale: Phase I (CYP450 oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis) vs phase II (conjugation) metabolism with the key inducers and inhibitors — shared page 252 with elimination-of-drugs, distinct subsections (the p196 shared-page convention).

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026

textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: VECTOR FLOW FIGURE (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed on ph3-vlm-census.ts): Lipophilic drugs → Phase I (predominantly CYP450-dependent) with the three reaction chutes Reduction / Oxidation / Hydrolysis → Slightly polar metabolite (active or inactive) + Reactive oxygen metabolites (label printed twice — at the phase I output and beside the phase II header) → Phase II with the four conjugation chutes Methylation / Acetylation / Glucuronidation / Sulfation → Very polar, hydrophilic metabolite (except acetylated metabolite) → Excretion: Serum (urine, sweat), bile (stool); the figure's second input, Polar drugs (water-soluble), bypasses phase I and feeds phase II directly. No margin notes or mnemonics.
textbookVisuals.kypLocation: the registry visual (MetabolismPhaseMap in visuals/pharm-p3.tsx — the pipeline zone with the input chips, bypass lane, CYP450 reactor, reactive-oxygen flag, conjugation station, except-acetylated chip, and excretion terminal) + blocks[2] the steps block distilling the same pipeline; the printed labels are also carried verbatim in blocks[1] the table block

textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed): 'Drugs can be metabolized by either or both phase I and phase II reactions. These reactions serve to bioactivate or deactivate substances, and do not have to take place sequentially (eg, phase I can follow phase II, or take place as a single reaction). topics.title: Elimination of Drugs: Zero & First Order
topics.productionRationale: Zero-order (capacity-limited, constant amount: ethanol, aspirin, phenytoin at therapeutic doses) vs first-order (constant fraction) elimination, the PEA/amount-over-time figure and the steady-state/half-life rules. Shared page 252 with drug-metabolism, distinct subsections.

topics.title: Urine pH, Ion Trapping & Dosage Calculations
topics.productionRationale: Weak acid/base ion trapping in urine (the aspirin overdose bicarbonate rule) + loading dose vs maintenance dose calculations with the Cp target equations.

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026

textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT + TYPESET EQUATIONS (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed): the rule 'Ionized species are trapped in urine and cleared quickly. Neutral forms can be reabsorbed.'; the weak-acid block (RCOOH (lipid soluble) ↔ RCOO– + H+ (trapped); examples phenobarbital, methotrexate, aspirin (salicylates); treat overdose with sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine); the weak-base block (RNH3+ (trapped) ↔ RNH2 + H+ (lipid soluble); examples TCAs, amphetamines; trapped in acidic environments; for severe alkalosis treat with ammonium chloride to acidify urine); the pKa definition (pH at which drugs (weak acid or base) are 50% ionized and 50% nonionized; represents the strength of the weak acid or base); the TCA rule (sodium bicarbonate to overcome the sodium channel-blocking activity — treats cardiac toxicity, does not accelerate drug elimination); and the dosage block (Loading dose = Cp × Vd / F; Maintenance dose = Cp × CL × τ / F; Cp = target plasma concentration; τ = dosage interval, does not apply for continuous infusions; renal/liver disease → maintenance dose ↓, loading dose usually unchanged; time to steady state depends primarily on t1/2, independent of dose and dosing frequency).

topics.title: Efficacy vs Potency: Reading Dose-Response Curves

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The two definition blocks (book 232): Efficacy (maximal effect a drug can produce — intrinsic activity; represented by the y-value (Emax); ↑ y-value = ↑ Emax = ↑ efficacy; unrelated to potency — efficacious drugs can have high or low potency; partial agonists have less efficacy than full agonists) and Potency (amount of drug needed for a given effect; represented by the x-value (EC50); left shifting = ↓ EC50 = ↑ potency = ↓ drug needed; unrelated to efficacy — potent drugs can have high or low efficacy)
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT (pdfimages: zero raster images): the page's entire text content is the two symmetric definition blocks, each carrying its own axis assignment (y-value Emax vs x-value EC50), its own conversion chain, its own independence clause, and — for efficacy only — the partial-agonist clause; the ↑/↓ arrows carry \x8f/\x90 control bytes in the raw text layer (stripped by norm).

topics.title: Drug Effect Modifications
topics.productionRationale: Potentiation, additive/synergistic effects, tolerance, tachyphylaxis, and the placebo/nocebo framework. Shared page 256 with autonomic-receptors, distinct subsections.

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The 6-row drug effect modifications table (book 234, top half) — TERM/DEFINITION/EXAMPLE for additive, permissive, synergistic, potentiation, antagonistic, tachyphylactic
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT TABLE (pdfimages: zero raster images on the page; no figures, no margin notes or mnemonics): one 6-row TERM/DEFINITION/EXAMPLE table — Additive (effect of substances A and B together is equal to the sum of their individual effects; aspirin and acetaminophen; “2 + 2 = 4”), Permissive (presence of substance A is required for the full effects of substance B; cortisol on catecholamine responsiveness; no chip), Synergistic (effect of substances A and B together is greater than the sum of their individual effects; clopidogrel with aspirin; “2 + 2 > 4”), Potentiation (similar to synergism, but drug B [with no therapeutic action alone] enhances the therapeutic action of drug A; carbidopa only blocks enzyme to prevent peripheral conversion of levodopa; “2 + 0 > 2”), Antagonistic (effect of substances A and B together is less than the sum of their individual effects; morphine with naloxone; “2 + 2 < 4”), Tachyphylactic (acute decrease in response to a drug after initial/repeated administration; repeat use of intranasal decongestant [eg, oxymetazoline] → ↓ therapeutic response [with rebound congestion]; no chip). textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The bladder innervation figure (book 236): the three nerve inputs, the two urethral sphincters, the four receptor placements, and the pontine retention-vs-voiding coordination
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: MIXED COMPOSITE FIGURE (pdfimages: THREE spot-color raster objects — 426x336, 383x518, 458x277 @316ppi — which the VLM reads as the white-silhouette anatomy layers of the bladder illustration: the bladder+lower-tract funnel, the valentine-shaped bladder body with the urethral stem, and the crescent lobulated detrusor wall band; all LABELS are live vector text): a coronal cutaway of the urinary bladder with a thick detrusor wall and folded mucosa, a funnel neck continuing as a vertical urethra, the internal urethral sphincter as two smooth ovoid masses at the bladder neck, and the external urethral sphincter as striated bundles lower on the urethra. Three yellow nerve lines enter from the left: Pelvic nerve (parasympathetic input) ending at the detrusor; Hypogastric nerve (sympathetic input) branching to the detrusor AND the bladder neck/internal sphincter; Pudendal nerve (somatic input) curving to the external urethral sphincter. Receptor labels with leader lines, each carrying a dark-teal numbered circle: M₃-receptor ❶ → detrusor; β₃-receptor ❷ → detrusor; α₁-receptor ❸ → internal urethral sphincter; plus Nicotinic receptor → external urethral sphincter. Beside the figure, a text panel carries the pons block — 'Micturition center in pons regulates involuntary bladder function via coordination of sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. ⊕ sympathetic → ↑ urinary retention. ⊕ parasympathetic → ↑ urine voiding. Some autonomic drugs act on smooth muscle receptors to treat bladder dysfunction.' — with the First Aid mnemonic 'Baby one more time.' printed directly below it (first letters B-o-m-t in the FA red; the page's own anchor is the red initials of the four example drugs in the table below).

topics.title: Autonomic Drugs: Synapse Targets & Overview
topics.productionRationale: The NE-release modulation (α2 autoreceptor negative feedback), amphetamine/VMAT/NET mechanism, and the cholinergic vs noradrenergic synapse figure with every drug's entry point (ChAT, botulinum, AChE, MAO, COMT, reserpine, guanethidine).

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The four-panel synapse figure (book 238): the cholinergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic synapses with every synthesis chain, transporter, cleft-clearance route, drug banner, and postsynaptic receptor — the master target map of autonomic pharmacology
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: VECTOR LINE ART, no raster (pdfimages: ZERO raster images on pdf 260, CONFIRMED; VLM available this session — four passes at 120 + 200 DPI including per-panel crops, saved to staging-ph15/vlm-census.txt): a page-dominating 2×2 grid of four synapse cartoons. CHOLINERGIC (top-left): ChAT joining Choline + Acetyl-CoA into ACh; vesicles; a Ca2+ channel with a green ⊕ to the release site; the red-bannered 'Cholinergic inhibitor — Botulinum toxin' whose red ⊖ terminates on the release machinery; the cleft enzyme AChE splitting ACh into Choline + Acetate; the green-bannered 'Cholinergic stimulant — AChE inhibitors eg, Donepezil' whose red ⊖ lands on AChE; postsynaptic M1, M2, M3 under 'Cholinoreceptors'. NORADRENERGIC (top-right): Tyrosine → DOPA → Dopamine in the cytoplasm, Dopamine → NE crossing the vesicle membrane via VMAT; 'Vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT) inhibitor — Tetrabenazine' (⊖ on VMAT); the 'Releasemodulating receptors' bracket grouping AT II (⊕) and α2 (⊖) with the dashed 'Negative feedback' curve from the cleft NE; 'Noradrenergic stimulant — Amphetamine, Ephedrine' (⊕ release); NET with its cleft→terminal 'Reuptake' arrow blocked by 'Noradrenergic stimulant — Amphetamine, SNRIs, Cocaine, TCAs, MDMA' (⊖ on NET); 'Diffusion, metabolism' leaving the cleft; postsynaptic α and β under 'Adrenoreceptors'; Ca2+ channel. SEROTONERGIC (bottom-right): Tryptophan → 5-Hydroxytryptophan → 5-HT; SERT + 'Reuptake' blocked by 'Serotonergic stimulant — Amphetamine, SNRIs, Cocaine, SSRIs' (⊖ on SERT); postsynaptic '5-HT receptor'; NO Ca2+, NO inhibitor banner. DOPAMINERGIC (bottom-left): Tyrosine → L-DOPA → Dopamine; DAT + 'Reuptake' blocked by 'Dopaminergic stimulant — Amphetamine, Methylphenidate, Cocaine' (⊖ on DAT); postsynaptic 'Dopamine receptor'; NO Ca2+, NO inhibitor banner. A small publisher logo prints at the lower right of the serotonergic panel (not reproduced).

topics.title: Specific Toxicity Treatments: The Antidote Table
topics.productionRationale: THE antidote table — acetaminophen (N-acetylcysteine), organophosphates (atropine + pralidoxime), methanol/ethylene glycol (fomepizole/dialysis), iron (deferoxamine), copper/arsenic/gold (dimercaprol), lead (EDTA/succimer), methemoglobinemia (methylene blue), cyanide (nitrite + thiosulfate), opioids, benzos, TCAs, warfarin, heparin — the highest-yield table in toxicology.

topics.title: Drug Reactions: Endocrine & Reproductive
topics.productionRationale: The endocrine/reproductive adverse-reaction table — from gynecomastia (spironolactone, cimetidine) to SIADH/hyponatremia (carbamazepine, SSRIs), adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism, and the sexual-dysfunction families.

topics.title: Drug Reactions: Hematologic
topics.productionRationale: The hematologic adverse-reaction table — aplastic anemia (chloramphenicol, carbamazepine), agranulocytosis (methimazole, clozapine), megaloblastic (methotrexate, phenytoin), hemolysis (G6PD drugs, penicillin, methyldopa), SLE-like, thrombocytopenia, and the gray-baby/serotonin-syndrome classics.

topics.title: Drug Reactions: Neurologic
topics.productionRationale: The neurologic adverse-reaction table — seizures (bupropion, INH, the withdrawn drugs), tremor/other movement disorders (tardive dyskinesia, Parkinsonism), headache, peripheral neuropathy (INH, vincristine, metronidazole), and the cognitive effects.

topics.title: Drugs Affecting Pupil Size & CYP-450 Interactions

topics.title: Drug Names: Prefixes, Suffixes & Stem Families
topics.productionRationale: The drug-name tables across both pages — the -prazole PPIs, -sartan ARBs, -olol β-blockers, -afil PDE-5s, -statin/-vastatin, gli- antidiabetics, -caine anesthetics, -pril ACEs, the dofa-/gab- families, and the suffix-to-class decoding rules.
